q: In Year 1 a railway earned Rs 4,00,000 crore with gross working expenses of Rs 3,60,000 crore. In Year 2 its earnings rose to Rs 4,40,000 crore but its gross working expenses rose to Rs 4,18,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio in Year 2, and the correct reading of the change, are:

options.A: 90%; performance has been maintained at the Year 1 level
options.B: 95%; performance has deteriorated despite the growth in earnings
options.C: 85%; performance has improved along with the earnings
options.D: 105%; the railway has slipped into an operating deficit

e: Year 2 Operating Ratio = Rs 4,18,000 / Rs 4,40,000 x 100 = 95 percent, up from 90 percent in Year 1, so performance deteriorated despite growth in earnings.

q: An improvement (lowering) of the Operating Ratio helps the Railways' finances most directly by:

options.A: Reducing the capital-at-charge on which the accounts are based
options.B: Doing away with the need for appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.C: Leaving a larger surplus out of earnings, which can be used to generate internal resources for purposes such as the Development Fund and capital investment through the Capital Fund
options.D: Automatically raising the fares and freight rates chargeable to the public

e: A lower Operating Ratio leaves a larger surplus out of earnings, which can generate internal resources for purposes such as the Development Fund and capital investment through the Capital Fund.

q: The Performance Efficiency Index (PEI) of a railway division is computed as:

options.A: Gross working expenses divided by gross (apportioned) earnings, multiplied by 100
options.B: Expenditure under the erstwhile Demands 3 to 12 divided by the originating earnings of the division, multiplied by 100
options.C: Net earnings divided by the capital-at-charge, multiplied by 100
options.D: Originating earnings divided by expenditure under the erstwhile Demands 3 to 12, multiplied by 100

e: PEI = expenditure under erstwhile Demands 3 to 12 / originating earnings of the division x 100, the divisional cost-centre measure.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the level at which the two performance indicators are worked out in railway practice?

options.A: The Operating Ratio is worked out for divisions and the Performance Efficiency Index for zonal railways
options.B: Both the indicators are worked out only for the Railways as a whole
options.C: Both the indicators are worked out only for individual stations
options.D: The Operating Ratio is worked out for zonal railways, which are treated as profit centres, while the Performance Efficiency Index is worked out for divisions, which are treated as cost centres

e: The Operating Ratio is worked out for zonal railways, treated as profit centres, while PEI is worked out for divisions, treated as cost centres.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Performance Efficiency Index is based on the originating earnings of the division.
2. The Operating Ratio of a zonal railway is based on its gross (apportioned) earnings.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: PEI is based on the division's originating earnings, while the zonal Operating Ratio is based on gross or apportioned earnings.

q: In computing the Performance Efficiency Index of a division, the items that are NOT taken into the expenditure side, unlike in the Operating Ratio, are:

options.A: Wages of staff working in the division
options.B: Appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund
options.C: Cost of fuel consumed in the division
options.D: Cost of stores consumed for repairs in the division

e: Unlike the Operating Ratio, PEI excludes appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund from the expenditure side.

q: The expenditure of a division under the erstwhile Demands 3 to 12 is Rs 480 crore and its originating earnings are Rs 800 crore. The Performance Efficiency Index of the division is:
e: PEI = expenditure / originating earnings x 100 = Rs 480 crore / Rs 800 crore x 100 = 60 percent.

q: A division reports a Performance Efficiency Index of 55% on originating earnings of Rs 1,200 crore. The expenditure taken into account for the index is:

options.A: Rs 540 crore
options.B: Rs 600 crore
options.C: Rs 660 crore
options.D: Rs 2,182 crore

e: Expenditure = PEI x originating earnings = 55 percent x Rs 1,200 crore = Rs 660 crore.

q: The Performance Efficiency Index of a division improves from 68% in one year to 62% in the next. This movement indicates that:

options.A: The division's expenditure has risen faster than its originating earnings
options.B: The division has necessarily earned a higher net profit, since divisions are profit centres
options.C: The index has worsened, since a fall in any performance index is unfavourable
options.D: The division now spends a smaller proportion of each rupee of its originating earnings, which is an improvement in its performance

e: A fall in PEI from 68 to 62 percent means the division now spends a smaller proportion of each rupee of originating earnings, which is an improvement.

q: A separate Performance Efficiency Index is used for divisions, instead of extending the zonal Operating Ratio to them as it stands, mainly because:

options.A: Divisions maintain no accounts of their expenditure at all
options.B: Apportioned earnings and items such as the appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund are not worked out at the divisional level, so a division cannot be judged like a zonal profit centre and is instead assessed on its own expenditure against its originating earnings
options.C: The Operating Ratio can be computed only once in five years
options.D: Divisions are not required to control their expenditure

e: Apportioned earnings and appropriations to DRF and Pension Fund are not worked out divisionally, so a division is assessed on its own expenditure against originating earnings, not as a profit centre.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Performance Efficiency Index:
1. It takes into account the expenditure under the erstwhile Demands 3 to 12 only.
2. It takes into account the appropriation to the Pension Fund in the expenditure of the division.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only: PEI takes expenditure under erstwhile Demands 3 to 12 only. Statement 2 is wrong as it excludes the appropriation to the Pension Fund.

q: The numerator used for the Performance Efficiency Index differs from that used for the Operating Ratio in that the index uses:

options.A: The gross working expenses, including appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund
options.B: The total capital expenditure of the division during the year
options.C: The net earnings of the division
options.D: Only the expenditure under the erstwhile Demands 3 to 12, leaving out the appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund

e: The PEI numerator uses only expenditure under erstwhile Demands 3 to 12, leaving out appropriations to DRF and Pension Fund, unlike the Operating Ratio numerator.

q: In railway traffic costing, the unit cost of freight service is obtained by:

options.A: Dividing the total cost of the freight service by the Net Tonne Kilometres (NTKM) performed
options.B: Dividing the total freight earnings by the tonnes originated
options.C: Dividing the total cost of all services by the train kilometres run
options.D: Dividing the Net Tonne Kilometres by the total cost of the freight service

e: Unit cost of freight service = total cost of the freight service / Net Tonne Kilometres performed.

q: The total cost attributable to a freight service is Rs 18,00,000 and the traffic carried is 30,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres. The unit cost of the service is:

options.A: Rs 6.00 per NTKM
options.B: Rs 1.67 per NTKM
options.C: Rs 0.60 per NTKM
options.D: Rs 0.06 per NTKM

e: Unit cost = Rs 18,00,000 / 30,00,000 NTKM = Rs 0.60 per NTKM.

q: The total cost of a coaching service is Rs 27,00,000 and the service produces 90,00,000 Passenger Kilometres. The unit cost of the service is:

options.A: Rs 3.00 per Passenger Kilometre
options.B: 3 paise per Passenger Kilometre
options.C: Rs 0.03 per Passenger Kilometre
options.D: 30 paise per Passenger Kilometre

e: Unit cost = Rs 27,00,000 / 90,00,000 Passenger Kilometres = Rs 0.30, that is 30 paise per Passenger Kilometre.

q: For a freight service, the earnings are 85 paise per NTKM and the unit cost is 68 paise per NTKM. The recovery of cost on the service is:
e: Recovery of cost = earnings / unit cost x 100 = 85 paise / 68 paise x 100 = 125 percent.

q: A workshop's total cost of a service remains unchanged while the volume of traffic units (NTKM) over which the cost is spread rises substantially. Other things being equal, the unit cost of the service will:

options.A: Fall, because the same total cost is now spread over a larger number of traffic units
options.B: Rise in the same proportion as the traffic units
options.C: Remain completely unaffected by the volume of traffic
options.D: Become equal to the total cost itself

e: With total cost unchanged and more traffic units to spread it over, unit cost = total cost / units falls.

q: Unit costs of the same service worked out for two zonal railways cannot be compared mechanically, without qualification, mainly because:

options.A: Unit costs are never expressed in money terms
options.B: The zones use different currencies in their cost accounts
options.C: Differences in the average lead of traffic, traffic density and operating conditions between the zones affect the unit cost independently of the efficiency of the managements concerned
options.D: Traffic costing is prepared only at the level of the Railways as a whole

e: Average lead, traffic density and operating conditions differ between zones and affect unit cost independently of management efficiency, so mechanical comparison is unsafe.

q: For judging whether a passenger service is covering its cost, the unit cost and the yield are most appropriately compared on the basis of:

options.A: Cost and earnings per train kilometre in both cases
options.B: Cost per Passenger Kilometre against earnings per Passenger Kilometre
options.C: Cost per route kilometre against total passenger earnings of the zone
options.D: Cost per coach against earnings per train

e: Covering of cost for a passenger service is judged by comparing cost per Passenger Kilometre against earnings per Passenger Kilometre, on the same unit basis.

q: The earnings per Passenger Kilometre of a coaching service are persistently well below its unit cost per Passenger Kilometre, while freight services earn well above their unit cost. In railway practice, the resulting position is that:

options.A: The coaching service is in fact the more profitable of the two
options.B: The unit cost of the coaching service must have been computed wrongly in every year
options.C: Both services should immediately be priced at exactly their unit costs
options.D: The loss on the coaching (passenger) service is borne by cross-subsidisation from the surplus earned on freight traffic

e: Coaching earnings below unit cost while freight earns above its unit cost means the passenger loss is borne by cross-subsidisation from the freight surplus.

q: A renewal of over-aged track is to be financed in one case, and a work of providing improved passenger amenities at a station in another. The funds ordinarily chargeable are, respectively:

options.A: Development Fund for the track renewal and Depreciation Reserve Fund for the passenger amenities
options.B: Depreciation Reserve Fund for the track renewal and Development Fund for the passenger amenities
options.C: Capital Fund for both the works
options.D: Pension Fund for both the works

e: Renewal of over-aged track is a renewal and replacement chargeable to the Depreciation Reserve Fund, while improved passenger amenities are financed from the Development Fund.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Capital Fund is used to finance asset-creating (capital) works of the Railways out of their own internal resources.
2. The Capital Fund is the fund out of which pensions are paid to retired railway staff.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only: the Capital Fund finances asset-creating capital works out of internal resources. Pensions are paid from the Pension Fund, not the Capital Fund.

q: A zonal railway proposes to meet the cost of a new asset-creating work from its own accumulated internal resources instead of from fresh budgetary support or market borrowing. The fund designed for financing such capital works out of internal resources is the:

options.A: Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.B: Pension Fund
options.C: Capital Fund
options.D: Railway Safety Fund

e: The Capital Fund is designed for financing asset-creating capital works out of the Railways' own accumulated internal resources.

q: In appraising the financial standing of the Railways, a finance officer notes that the appropriation to the Depreciation Reserve Fund has remained inadequate for several years. The most likely consequence for asset management is:

options.A: An immediate improvement in the Operating Ratio with no other effect
options.B: A fall in the capital-at-charge to nil
options.C: An automatic increase in the balance of the Development Fund
options.D: Accumulation of arrears of renewal and replacement of over-aged assets, with renewals falling due faster than they can be financed

e: Inadequate DRF appropriation over years leads to accumulation of arrears of renewal and replacement of over-aged assets, with renewals falling due faster than they can be financed.

q: Which of the following sets of works is ordinarily financed from the Development Fund of the Railways?

options.A: Renewal and replacement of worn-out assets
options.B: Passenger amenities, labour welfare works and unremunerative operational improvements
options.C: Payment of pensions and gratuities
options.D: Repayment of market borrowings raised through IRFC

e: The Development Fund ordinarily finances passenger amenities, labour welfare works and unremunerative operational improvements, not renewals, pensions or loan repayment.

q: A balance standing at the credit of a railway fund such as the Depreciation Reserve Fund or the Development Fund at the close of a financial year:

options.A: Does not lapse; it is carried forward in the Public Account for use in the following years
options.B: Lapses in the same way as the unspent balance of a grant
options.C: Is automatically transferred to the Consolidated Fund of India as revenue
options.D: Must be refunded to the passengers and freight customers of the year

e: A balance at credit of a railway fund like DRF or Development Fund does not lapse; it is carried forward in the Public Account for use in following years.

q: The gross earnings of the Railways for a year are Rs 5,00,000 crore and the total working expenses, including the appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund, are Rs 4,60,000 crore. The net revenue of the Railways for the year is:

options.A: Rs 9,60,000 crore
options.B: Rs 4,60,000 crore
options.C: Rs 40,000 crore
options.D: Rs 5,00,000 crore

e: Net revenue = gross earnings - total working expenses including DRF and Pension Fund appropriations = Rs 5,00,000 - Rs 4,60,000 = Rs 40,000 crore.

q: Under the pre-merger arrangement, where the net revenue of the Railways in a year was insufficient to pay the full dividend due to General Revenues on the capital-at-charge, the unpaid portion of the dividend was carried to the:

options.A: Development Fund
options.B: Contingency Fund of India
options.C: Railway Safety Fund
options.D: Deferred Dividend Liability Account

e: Under the pre-merger arrangement, the unpaid portion of dividend due to General Revenues was carried to the Deferred Dividend Liability Account.

q: A company's Earnings Per Share are Rs 16 and the dividend declared is Rs 4 per share. Its dividend payout ratio is:
e: Dividend payout ratio = dividend per share / EPS x 100 = Rs 4 / Rs 16 x 100 = 25 percent.

q: A company's Dividend Per Share is Rs 7 and the market price of its share is Rs 140. Its dividend yield ratio is:
e: Dividend yield = Dividend Per Share / market price x 100 = Rs 7 / Rs 140 x 100 = 5 percent.

q: A lender appraising the financial standing of an enterprise before sanctioning a long-term loan would rely most directly on a combination of:

options.A: The gross profit ratio and the inventory turnover ratio alone
options.B: The dividend yield ratio and the Earnings Per Share alone
options.C: The debt-equity ratio, which shows the proportion of outside debt to owners' funds, and the interest coverage ratio, which shows how comfortably its earnings cover the interest payable
options.D: The current ratio alone, ignoring all long-term obligations

e: A long-term lender relies most directly on the debt-equity ratio for the debt-to-owners' funds proportion and the interest coverage ratio for how comfortably earnings cover interest.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 8,400 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 1,40,000 crore. The return on the capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = net earnings / capital-at-charge x 100 = Rs 8,400 / Rs 1,40,000 x 100 = 6 percent.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 7,50,000 and the interest payable by it is Rs 2,50,000. Its interest coverage ratio, as a measure of its financial standing, is:

options.A: 0.33 times
options.B: 1 time
options.C: 10 times
options.D: 3 times

e: Interest coverage = profit before interest and tax / interest = Rs 7,50,000 / Rs 2,50,000 = 3 times.

q: The anticipated rate of return on a proposed railway work, computed on its initial estimated cost, works out to 8%. Judged by the prescribed test of remunerativeness, the work is:

options.A: Unremunerative, as it falls short of the minimum return of 10% required for a work to be financially justified
options.B: Remunerative, as any positive return satisfies the test
options.C: Remunerative, as the test requires a return of only 6%
options.D: Exempt from appraisal, as returns below 10% need no examination

e: A return of 8 percent falls short of the minimum 10 percent required for a work to be financially justified, so the work is unremunerative under the prescribed test.

q: Under the pre-merger arrangement, after the dividend due to General Revenues had been provided for out of the net revenue of the Railways, the surplus that remained was ordinarily disposed of by appropriations to:

options.A: The Contingency Fund of India and the Public Account only
options.B: The wages and allowances heads of the working expenses
options.C: Funds such as the Development Fund and the Capital Fund, for financing the Railways' own development and capital works
options.D: The general revenues of the State Governments through which the lines passed

e: After providing dividend to General Revenues, the remaining surplus was ordinarily appropriated to funds such as the Development Fund and Capital Fund for the Railways' own works.

q: A standard cost card drawn up for a manufactured product normally records, for one unit of the product:

options.A: Only the actual cost incurred on the last batch produced
options.B: The standard quantity and standard price of each material, the standard time and standard rate for each labour operation, and the standard overhead charge
options.C: Only the selling price at which the unit is expected to be sold
options.D: The names of the workers who are to produce the unit

e: A standard cost card records for one unit the standard quantity and price of each material, standard time and rate for each labour operation, and the standard overhead charge.

q: Standards for material quantities, labour times and prices are most reliably set when they are fixed:

options.A: By the stores clerk alone, from the balances in the stock ledger
options.B: By copying the actual results of the single best month in the past
options.C: Jointly, by the engineering, production, purchase, personnel and accounts staff concerned, using work study and current price information
options.D: By the external auditor as part of the statutory audit

e: Standards are most reliably set jointly by engineering, production, purchase, personnel and accounts staff, using work study and current price information.

q: A basic standard in standard costing is a standard which:

options.A: Is left unchanged over a long period and is used mainly to show the trend of efficiency over the years
options.B: Is revised at the end of every week of production
options.C: Represents a level of performance that is perfect and attainable in every respect
options.D: Is set only for the material element of cost

e: A basic standard is left unchanged over a long period and is used mainly to show the trend of efficiency over the years, not for current control.

q: The standards in force in a factory should ordinarily be revised when:

options.A: A single day's production falls below the standard output
options.B: A worker asks for the standard to be made easier
options.C: The variance in one month happens to be favourable
options.D: There is a permanent change in material prices, wage rates, methods of production or the design of the product

e: Standards should be revised when there is a permanent change in material prices, wage rates, methods of production or product design, not for temporary fluctuations.

q: Standard costing gives its best results in an undertaking where:

options.A: Every order is a one-off job made to a customer's special design
options.B: Production is of standardised products by repetitive processes, so that the same operations and materials recur and standards can be applied uniformly
options.C: No cost records of any kind are maintained
options.D: Output cannot be measured in physical units at all

e: Standard costing works best where production is of standardised products by repetitive processes, so the same operations and materials recur and standards apply uniformly.

q: A practical difficulty in operating a standard costing system in a period of rapidly changing prices and technology is that:

options.A: Variances can never be calculated in such a period
options.B: Actual costs cease to be recorded in such a period
options.C: Standards become out of date quickly and need frequent revision, which adds to the cost and work of running the system
options.D: Standard costing can be used only for labour costs in such a period

e: In rapidly changing prices and technology, standards become out of date quickly and need frequent revision, adding to the cost and work of running the system.

q: In a variance report, the material price variance is normally brought to the notice of the purchasing function chiefly because:

options.A: That function is responsible for the price negotiated and paid for materials, as distinct from the quantity consumed in production
options.B: That function fixes the standard time for each operation
options.C: That function supervises the workers on the shop floor
options.D: That function prepares the sales budget of the enterprise

e: Material price variance is reported to the purchasing function because it is responsible for the price negotiated and paid, as distinct from quantity consumed in production.

q: Excess consumption of material over the standard quantity for the output obtained points, for control purposes, primarily to the need to enquire into:

options.A: The price at which the material was bought
options.B: The dividend declared by the enterprise
options.C: The selling price charged to customers
options.D: Shop-floor causes such as wastage, spoilage, defective material handling and the quality of material issued

e: Excess material consumption over standard quantity points to shop-floor causes such as wastage, spoilage, defective handling and quality of material issued.

q: The labour mix (gang composition) variance arises when:

options.A: The wage rate paid differs from the standard wage rate
options.B: The actual proportion of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers in the gang differs from the standard proportion laid down for the work
options.C: Time is lost through a power failure in the factory
options.D: More units are produced than were budgeted for the period

e: Labour mix variance arises when the actual proportion of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers in the gang differs from the standard proportion laid down.

q: A revision variance in standard costing is the variance which arises because:

options.A: The workers take longer than the standard time for a job
options.B: More material is consumed than the standard quantity
options.C: The original standard itself has been revised during the period, so part of the difference between the original and actual cost is due to the change in the standard
options.D: The actual overheads exceed the absorbed overheads

e: Revision variance arises because the original standard itself was revised during the period, so part of the difference from actual cost is due to the change in standard.

q: The fixed overhead expenditure (spending) variance measures:

options.A: The difference between the budgeted fixed overheads for the period and the actual fixed overheads incurred
options.B: The difference caused by producing more or fewer units than budgeted
options.C: The difference caused by working on more days than the budgeted number of days
options.D: The difference between the fixed and the variable overheads of the period

e: Fixed overhead expenditure variance = budgeted fixed overheads for the period - actual fixed overheads incurred; it measures spending, not output volume.

q: The fixed overhead volume variance arises essentially because:

options.A: More was spent on fixed overheads than was budgeted
options.B: The price of materials rose during the period
options.C: The wage rates paid were higher than the standard rates
options.D: The actual output differs from the budgeted output over which the fixed overheads were to be absorbed, so the overheads are over-absorbed or under-absorbed

e: Fixed overhead volume variance arises because actual output differs from budgeted output over which fixed overheads were to be absorbed, causing over- or under-absorption.

q: A calendar variance in overhead analysis arises when:

options.A: The wage rate for a grade of labour is revised
options.B: The actual number of working days in the period differs from the number of days budgeted, so the capacity available differs from the budgeted capacity
options.C: The actual price of power differs from the standard price
options.D: The output of one day is sold at a discount

e: Calendar variance arises when the actual number of working days differs from the budgeted number, so capacity available differs from budgeted capacity.

q: The variable overhead efficiency variance is broadly the part of the variable overhead variance which arises because:

options.A: The actual variable overheads spent differ from the budget allowance for the actual hours worked
options.B: The fixed overheads of the period were under-absorbed
options.C: The actual hours taken for the output differ from the standard hours allowed for it, valued at the standard variable overhead rate
options.D: The number of working days in the month has changed

e: Variable overhead efficiency variance is the difference between actual hours taken and standard hours allowed for the output, valued at the standard variable overhead rate.

q: Before a reported variance is taken up for detailed investigation, the consideration that should weigh most with management, besides its size, is:

options.A: Whether the expected benefit of finding and removing its cause is likely to exceed the cost of the investigation, and whether the variance is of a controllable and recurring kind
options.B: The colour in which the variance report is printed
options.C: Whether the variance happens to be favourable rather than adverse
options.D: The number of pages in the variance report

e: Besides size, investigation should depend on whether the expected benefit of finding and removing the cause is likely to exceed the investigation cost, and whether it is controllable and recurring.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes standard costing from budgetary control?

options.A: Standard costing deals with totals for a department, while budgetary control deals only with cost per unit
options.B: Neither of them makes any use of predetermined figures
options.C: Standard costing is a technique of cost control applied mainly to the cost per unit of a product or operation, while budgetary control plans and controls the operations of the whole enterprise or its departments in total, through budgets
options.D: Budgetary control is a part of the double-entry system, while standard costing is not a costing technique at all

e: Standard costing controls cost per unit of a product or operation, while budgetary control plans and controls total operations of the whole enterprise or departments through budgets.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A forecast is an estimate of what is likely to happen in a future period, given the conditions expected to prevail.
2. A budget goes beyond a forecast; it is a plan, approved as policy, which management is expected to work to and against which performance is measured.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: A forecast only estimates likely future events, whereas a budget is an approved plan and policy target against which actual performance is measured, so both statements are correct.

q: A budget centre is best described as:

options.A: A section of the organisation, such as a department, a workshop or a cost centre, for which a separate budget is prepared and over whose performance a named manager is held responsible
options.B: The office in which the master budget is finally printed
options.C: A bank account in which the budgeted funds are kept
options.D: The committee which approves the annual budget

e: A budget centre is a defined section like a department or workshop for which a separate budget is prepared and a named manager is held responsible for its performance.

q: The main work of a budget officer in a budgetary control system is to:

options.A: Personally carry out the production work of every department
options.B: Fix the selling prices of all the products of the enterprise
options.C: Audit the annual accounts of the enterprise
options.D: Co-ordinate the preparation of the functional budgets, issue the budget timetable and guidance, and consolidate and report budget performance

e: The budget officer co-ordinates functional budgets, issues the timetable and guidance, consolidates them and reports performance; he does not himself do production or audit work.

q: The sales of a factory could be greatly increased, but a single scarce grade of alloy steel is in short supply and limits the output that can be made. In preparing the budgets for the year, the factor to be planned around first is:

options.A: The sales demand, ignoring the shortage of steel
options.B: The supply of the scarce alloy steel, since it is the principal (key) budget factor governing the level of activity of the whole enterprise
options.C: The advertisement budget of the enterprise
options.D: The dividend expected by the shareholders

e: The scarce alloy steel is the principal or key budget factor because it limits output, so all other budgets must first be planned around its available supply.

q: The production budget of a manufacturing enterprise is drawn up primarily:

options.A: Only in terms of the money value of production
options.B: Only after the cash budget has been finally approved
options.C: In physical units of each product to be produced, from which the material, labour and overhead budgets are then worked out
options.D: By the selling department without reference to stocks

e: The production budget is first drawn in physical units for each product, and the material, labour and overhead budgets are then derived from those quantities.

q: The materials purchase budget cannot be prepared in isolation, mainly because:

options.A: It depends on the quantities required by the production budget and on the opening stock, the stock to be carried at the close and the lead time for supplies
options.B: It is prepared by the sales department
options.C: Purchases are always made for cash only
options.D: Material prices never change during a year

e: Purchases depend on production requirements plus closing stock minus opening stock, also allowing for lead time, so the purchase budget cannot be fixed in isolation.

q: Once the master budget has been approved, it serves management chiefly as:

options.A: A substitute for the annual financial statements
options.B: A document to be filed away without further reference during the year
options.C: A record of the results actually achieved in the previous year
options.D: The approved summary plan for the period, authorising the functional plans it consolidates and providing the standard against which actual performance is compared

e: Once approved, the master budget is the summary plan authorising functional plans and serving as the standard against which actual performance is compared.

q: Capital expenditure on a large project is commonly budgeted over a longer horizon than the annual revenue budget mainly because:

options.A: Capital projects are not subject to any control
options.B: Such projects are planned, executed and completed over several years, and their costs and benefits extend well beyond a single budget year
options.C: The annual budget is prepared only for the sales department
options.D: Capital expenditure is always met from revenue receipts

e: Capital projects are executed over several years and give benefits beyond one year, so their expenditure is budgeted over a longer horizon than the annual revenue budget.

q: A budget manual is a document which:

options.A: Contains only the final figures of the master budget
options.B: Is issued only to the statutory auditors of the enterprise
options.C: Records the actual expenditure incurred in the previous year
options.D: Sets out the budget procedure — the responsibilities of each manager, the timetable for preparing budgets, the forms to be used and the manner of reporting performance

e: A budget manual lays down procedure: responsibilities of managers, timetable, forms to be used and how performance is to be reported.

q: In reporting budget performance to a departmental manager, sound practice requires that the report should:

options.A: Charge the manager with every cost incurred in his department, whether or not he can influence it
options.B: Separately show the costs he can control, so that his performance is judged on controllable items, while uncontrollable items are shown only for information
options.C: Omit all unfavourable items from his report
options.D: Be sent to him only at the end of the financial year

e: A manager should be judged on controllable costs shown separately; uncontrollable items are shown only for information, otherwise appraisal would be unfair.

q: Budgetary control fits in with responsibility accounting because:

options.A: Both are concerned only with the preparation of the annual accounts
options.B: Neither of them requires costs to be collected by departments
options.C: Budgets can be prepared for the whole enterprise in one lump sum
options.D: Budgets are drawn up by responsibility (budget) centres, and the actual results of each centre are compared with its budget to judge the manager responsible for that centre

e: Budgets are set by responsibility centres and actuals of each centre are compared with its budget to judge its manager, which is exactly responsibility accounting.

q: Allowing the managers who will have to work to a budget to take a real part in preparing it generally helps the system because:

options.A: It removes the need for any comparison of actuals with the budget
options.B: Such managers possess first-hand knowledge of their operations and are more committed to targets they have helped to set
options.C: It guarantees that the budget will always be achieved in full
options.D: It dispenses with the need for approval of the master budget

e: Managers who help prepare their budget know operations first-hand and feel committed to targets they helped set, so participation improves acceptance and control.

q: A budget imposed from above, without consulting the managers who must achieve it and without regard to the conditions in their departments, is likely to fail mainly because:

options.A: Its figures are printed in too much detail
options.B: It covers a period of one year
options.C: The managers concerned feel no commitment to it and may regard its targets as unrealistic, so co-operation and control both suffer
options.D: It is prepared before the start of the budget period

e: An imposed budget without consultation feels unrealistic to managers, earns no commitment or co-operation, and therefore budgetary control suffers.

q: For budgetary control reports to be effective at different levels of management, they should be:

options.A: Identical in detail for every level, from the foreman to the board
options.B: Prepared only when a manager specifically demands one
options.C: Sent only to the accounts department
options.D: Prompt and graded to the level receiving them — detailed for the manager who must act on them, and progressively summarised for higher levels

e: Reports must be prompt and graded: detailed for the manager who must act, and progressively summarised for higher levels of management.

q: Actual output in a period turns out to be well below the level assumed in the original budget. For a fair control comparison, the actual costs should be compared with:

options.A: The flexed budget allowance for the actual level of output, so that the effect of the change in activity is separated from the efficiency of cost control
options.B: The original budget allowance, without any adjustment for the fall in output
options.C: The actual costs of the corresponding period of last year only
options.D: The budget of a different department of the same size

e: Actual costs should be compared with the flexed budget for actual output, so volume effects are separated from real efficiency in cost control.

q: A flexible budget is ordinarily drawn up:

options.A: For one fixed level of activity only
options.B: For a range of levels of activity, showing the expected cost at each level, so that the allowance for the level actually attained can be taken from it
options.C: Only after the actual results of the year are fully known
options.D: Only for the selling department of an enterprise

e: A flexible budget shows expected cost at a range of activity levels, allowing the correct allowance for the level actually attained to be picked.

q: A manager is judged against a fixed budget prepared for 20,000 units, although only 14,000 units could be produced because demand fell. The main defect in using that fixed budget for judging him is that:

options.A: A fixed budget contains no fixed costs at all
options.B: Fixed budgets are never expressed in money terms
options.C: Much of the difference between the budget and the actuals is caused by the change in the volume of activity itself, and not by how well or badly he controlled costs at the level actually worked
options.D: The manager was not informed of the budget in advance

e: With a fixed budget, much variance is caused merely by volume change from 20,000 to 14,000 units, not by the manager's cost control, so judgement is unfair.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 60,000 for a period and a variable cost of Rs 25 per unit. The flexed budget allowance for an output of 3,000 units is:
e: Flexed allowance = fixed Rs 60,000 + variable Rs 25 x 3,000 = Rs 60,000 + Rs 75,000 = Rs 1,35,000.

q: Zero-base budgeting differs from the traditional incremental method of budgeting in that it:

options.A: Starts from the previous year's budget and adds a percentage for expected increases
options.B: Requires every activity, old as well as new, to be justified afresh for the budget period as if it were being taken up for the first time, instead of accepting the previous year's level as the base
options.C: Is prepared only for the cash position of the enterprise
options.D: Does away with the need to rank competing demands on resources

e: Zero-base budgeting requires every activity, old or new, to be justified afresh from zero, instead of accepting last year's level as the base.

q: The chief weakness of incremental budgeting, which zero-base budgeting seeks to remove, is that:

options.A: It carries forward the costs, inefficiencies and outdated activities of the previous years into the new budget, because only the increase over the past level is examined closely
options.B: It requires the budget to be prepared before the year begins
options.C: It expresses the budget in money terms
options.D: It involves the departmental managers in preparing estimates

e: Incremental budgeting only scrutinises the increase, so past inefficiencies and outdated activities are carried forward unexamined into the new budget.

q: After the decision packages of the several departments have been prepared under zero-base budgeting, the next essential step is to:

options.A: Approve every package in full, in the order in which it is received
options.B: Discard the packages and return to the previous year's figures
options.C: Rank the packages in order of priority according to their benefits in relation to their costs, and allot the available funds down the ranking until they are exhausted
options.D: Divide the available funds equally among all the departments

e: Decision packages are ranked by benefit relative to cost and funds are allotted down the ranking until available funds are exhausted.

q: Zero-base budgeting is found particularly suitable for:

options.A: Direct material costs, which vary strictly with output
options.B: The interest payable on loans already raised
options.C: Statutory payments which the enterprise is bound to make in full
options.D: Staff and support (discretionary) activities such as administration, research and training, whose output is not easily measured and whose level of service is a matter of managerial choice

e: Zero-base budgeting suits discretionary staff and support activities like administration, research and training, where service level is a managerial choice.

q: A recognised drawback of zero-base budgeting in practice is that it:

options.A: Cannot be applied to any government or service organisation
options.B: Is very time-consuming and generates a large volume of paperwork and decision packages, needing trained managers to prepare and evaluate them
options.C: Requires no justification of any activity at all
options.D: Always results in the closure of the departments reviewed

e: Zero-base budgeting is time-consuming and paperwork-heavy, with many decision packages needing trained managers to prepare and evaluate them.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 40 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 38 per kg. The actual quantity purchased and consumed is 300 kg. The material price variance is:

options.A: Rs 600 adverse
options.B: Rs 11,400 favourable
options.C: Rs 600 favourable
options.D: Rs 12,000 favourable

e: Material price variance = (standard price - actual price) x actual quantity = (Rs 40 - Rs 38) x 300 kg = Rs 600 favourable.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time allowed is 800 hours, while the actual time taken is 750 hours. The standard wage rate is Rs 50 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 2,500 favourable
options.B: Rs 2,500 adverse
options.C: Rs 37,500 favourable
options.D: Rs 40,000 favourable

e: Labour efficiency variance = (standard hours - actual hours) x standard rate = (800 - 750) x Rs 50 = Rs 2,500 favourable.

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a department for a period are Rs 90,000 and the actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 96,000. The fixed overhead expenditure variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 favourable
options.B: Rs 90,000 adverse
options.C: Nil
options.D: Rs 6,000 adverse

e: Fixed overhead expenditure variance = budgeted Rs 90,000 - actual Rs 96,000 = Rs 6,000 adverse, as actual spending exceeded budget.

q: At the end of a period, the variances disclosed by a standard costing system which are significant are ordinarily disposed of by:

options.A: Carrying every variance forward indefinitely in the stock accounts
options.B: Transferring them to the costing profit and loss account of the period, so that the reported profit reflects the efficiencies and inefficiencies of the period
options.C: Debiting them to the personal accounts of the workers concerned
options.D: Ignoring them, since standard costs alone are shown in the accounts

e: Significant variances are transferred to the costing profit and loss account so reported profit reflects the period's efficiencies and inefficiencies.

q: In reporting the performance of the selling function, it is most useful to separate the sales variance into its price and volume parts because:

options.A: A shortfall caused by selling fewer units calls for a different enquiry and remedy from a shortfall caused by realising lower prices than standard
options.B: Sales variances have no connection with the profit of the enterprise
options.C: The two parts are always equal in amount
options.D: The volume part of the variance is never reported to management

e: Splitting sales variance into price and volume shows whether shortfall came from fewer units or lower prices, each needing a different remedy.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Standard costing and budgetary control support each other: the standards provide the unit rates from which many budget figures are built up, and the budgets provide the planned level of activity at which the standards are to operate.
2. Either system, once installed, makes the other wholly unnecessary.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Standards supply unit rates for building budgets and budgets set the activity level for standards, so they support each other; neither makes the other unnecessary.

q: The cost of retained earnings is described as an implicit (opportunity) cost because:

options.A: A fixed rate of interest is payable on retained earnings to the debenture holders
options.B: No outlay is made for using them, yet the shareholders forgo the return they could have earned by investing the distributed profit elsewhere
options.C: Retained earnings have to be repaid to the shareholders on a fixed date
options.D: The company must obtain the permission of the Registrar before using them

e: Retained earnings involve no outlay, but shareholders forgo returns they could earn elsewhere on distributed profit, making it an implicit opportunity cost.

q: The target capital structure of an enterprise is 55% equity (cost 14%), 15% preference capital (cost 10%) and 30% debt (after-tax cost 8%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
In computing the weighted average cost of capital, the cost of debt is taken after tax, whereas no such tax adjustment is made to the cost of equity, because:

options.A: Interest on debt is an allowable charge against taxable profits and so reduces the tax payable, while dividend on shares is an appropriation of after-tax profits
options.B: Debt capital is always raised for a shorter period than equity capital
options.C: The rate of interest on debt is fixed by the Government
options.D: Equity shares carry no risk for their holders

e: Interest is tax-deductible and reduces tax payable, so debt cost is taken after tax; dividends are paid from after-tax profit, so no adjustment is made for equity.

q: A company issues 12% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 125 per share. The shares are irredeemable. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of irredeemable preference capital = dividend / issue price = Rs 12 / Rs 125 = 9.6%.

q: The dividend expected on a share next year is Rs 9 per share, its current market price is Rs 60 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 3% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = expected dividend / price + growth = Rs 9 / Rs 60 + 3% = 15% + 3% = 18%.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, the risk-free rate is 4%, the expected return on the market portfolio is 12% and the beta of a share is 1.25. The cost of equity of the share is:
Under the Net Income approach to capital structure, it is assumed that the cost of equity remains constant while cheaper debt replaces equity, so that as the proportion of debt rises:

options.A: The overall cost of capital falls and the value of the firm rises
options.B: The overall cost of capital rises and the value of the firm falls
options.C: The overall cost of capital remains unchanged at all levels of debt
options.D: The value of the firm depends only on its operating risk

e: Under Net Income approach, constant equity cost plus cheaper debt lowers overall cost of capital and raises firm value as debt proportion rises.

q: A company issues 14% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 112 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of this debt is:
e: Cost of debt ignoring tax = annual interest / proceeds = Rs 14 / Rs 112 = 12.5%.

q: Book-value weights are considered an unreliable basis for computing the weighted average cost of capital mainly because:

options.A: Book values are not available from the balance sheet of a company
options.B: Book values record historical amounts and may differ widely from the current economic values of the different sources of finance
options.C: Book values give too much weight to debt capital in every case
options.D: Book values change every day with the market price of the shares

e: Book values are historical and may differ widely from current economic values, so weights based on them do not reflect present financing proportions.

q: The weighted average cost of capital of an enterprise is 13.6%. Its cost of equity is 16% and its after-tax cost of debt is 10%. The proportion of equity in its capital structure is:

An enterprise earns a return on its total capital employed which is lower than the rate of interest payable on its borrowings. If it increases the proportion of debt in its capital structure, the effect will be:

options.A: A fall in the earnings available to the equity shareholders, because the enterprise earns less on the borrowed funds than the interest it must pay on them
options.B: A rise in the earnings per share in every such case
options.C: No effect at all on the equity shareholders
options.D: An automatic reduction in the rate of interest on the borrowings

e: If return on capital is below interest rate, borrowed funds earn less than interest payable, reducing earnings left for equity shareholders.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 12,50,000 and pays interest of Rs 2,50,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - interest) = Rs 12,50,000 / Rs 10,00,000 = 1.25.

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 48,00,000, its variable costs are Rs 30,00,000 and its fixed operating costs are Rs 10,00,000. Its degree of operating leverage is:
The degree of operating leverage of an enterprise is 2.4 and its degree of financial leverage is 1.5. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = DOL x DFL = 2.4 x 1.5 = 3.6.

q: A workshop replaces manual operations by an automated plant, so that its fixed costs rise sharply while its variable cost per unit falls. Other things being equal, the workshop will now show:

options.A: A higher break-even point and a higher degree of operating leverage, its profit becoming more sensitive to changes in the volume of work
options.B: A lower break-even point and a lower degree of operating leverage
options.C: No change in its break-even point, since total cost is unchanged
options.D: A degree of operating leverage of exactly one

e: Automation raises fixed costs and lowers unit variable cost, raising break-even and operating leverage, so profit becomes more sensitive to volume.

q: A company needs total funds of Rs 20,00,000, raised in shares of Rs 10 each. Under Plan A the whole amount is raised as equity (2,00,000 shares). Under Plan B, Rs 10,00,000 is raised by debt at 12% interest and the balance as equity (1,00,000 shares). Ignoring tax, the indifference point, that is, the level of earnings before interest and tax at which the earnings per share are the same under both plans, is:
e: Set EPS equal: EBIT / 2,00,000 = (EBIT - Rs 1,20,000) / 1,00,000, giving EBIT = Rs 2,40,000 as the indifference point.

q: A proposed project carries a risk distinctly higher than the average risk of the enterprise's existing operations. In appraising such a project, the correct treatment of the discount rate is to:

options.A: Use the overall cost of capital of the enterprise without any change
options.B: Use the rate of interest paid on the last loan raised by the enterprise
options.C: Discount the project at the risk-free rate of return
options.D: Use a higher, risk-adjusted discount rate reflecting the risk of the project itself, instead of the average cost of capital of the enterprise

e: A higher-risk project must be discounted at a higher risk-adjusted rate reflecting its own risk, not the firm's average cost of capital.

q: 'Financial risk' borne by the equity shareholders of an enterprise refers to:

options.A: The risk that the sales of the enterprise will fall in a recession
options.B: The risk arising from changes in the prices of the raw materials it uses
options.C: The additional variability of their earnings, and the risk of insolvency, created by the fixed financial charges on debt and preference capital in the capital structure
options.D: The risk that the market price of its shares will fall on the stock exchange

e: Financial risk is the extra variability of equity earnings and insolvency risk created by fixed charges on debt and preference capital.

q: An enterprise expects retained earnings of Rs 6,40,000 to be available for investment during the year. In its target capital structure, equity forms 40% of the total capital. The break point of its marginal cost of capital schedule, that is, the total fresh capital it can raise before it must issue new equity shares, is:
e: Break point = retained earnings / equity weight = Rs 6,40,000 / 0.40 = Rs 16,00,000 of total fresh capital before new equity is needed.

q: A company is said to be highly geared when:

options.A: Its current assets are much larger than its current liabilities
options.B: The proportion of fixed-charge capital, namely debt and preference capital, is high in relation to its equity share capital
options.C: It has issued no preference shares at all
options.D: Its reserves and surplus exceed its share capital

e: A highly geared company has a high proportion of fixed-charge capital, debt and preference capital, relative to equity share capital.
